topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The federal Fair Housing Act is officially known as Title VIII of which piece of legislation?
choice_a: The Civil Rights Act of 1968
choice_b: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
choice_c: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988
choice_d: The Community Reinvestment Act of 1977
explanation: The federal Fair Housing Act is Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968. It was later amended in 1988 (the Fair Housing Amendments Act) to add disability and familial status as protected classes.
source_note: DOJ Civil Rights Division, Fair Housing Act overview (justice.gov/crt/fair-housing-act-1); Wikipedia, Civil Rights Act of 1968.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: What is the correct United States Code citation for the federal Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: 42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.
choice_b: 15 U.S.C. § 1 et seq.
choice_c: 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.
choice_d: 12 U.S.C. § 2601 et seq.
explanation: The federal Fair Housing Act is codified at 42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq. (15 U.S.C. § 1 is the Sherman Antitrust Act; 42 U.S.C. § 12101 is the ADA; 12 U.S.C. § 2601 is RESPA.)
source_note: DOJ Civil Rights Division, Fair Housing Act overview (justice.gov/crt/fair-housing-act-1).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which federal agency has primary administrative and enforcement responsibility for the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
choice_b: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
choice_c: The Department of Labor
choice_d: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
explanation: HUD's Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity (FHEO) administers and enforces the Fair Housing Act, investigating complaints and, together with the Department of Justice, pursuing enforcement actions.
source_note: HUD.gov, Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity; DOJ Civil Rights Division.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: In what year were disability and familial status added as protected classes under the federal Fair Housing Act?
explanation: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added disability and familial status to the original 1968 Act's protected classes of race, color, religion, and national origin (sex was added in 1974).
source_note: Wikipedia, Civil Rights Act of 1968 (Title VIII); DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which seven classes are explicitly protected under the federal Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability
choice_b: Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, marital status, and sexual orientation
choice_c: Race, religion, national origin, disability, age, income source, and marital status
choice_d: Race, color, sex, familial status, disability, sexual orientation, and gender identity
explanation: The seven classes explicitly protected under the federal Fair Housing Act are race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability. Marital status, sexual orientation, and gender identity are not explicitly enumerated in the federal statute, though some are protected under state or local laws.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A landlord advertises a rental and, when questioned, admits he will not rent to unmarried couples living together. Under the federal Fair Housing Act alone, is this a violation?
choice_a: No, because marital status is not one of the seven classes explicitly protected under the federal Act
choice_b: Yes, because marital status is one of the seven federally protected classes
choice_c: Yes, because this always constitutes familial status discrimination
choice_d: No, because landlords may refuse any applicant for any reason
explanation: Marital status is not among the seven classes protected under the federal Fair Housing Act, so this refusal, standing alone, would not violate federal law (though many states and localities separately prohibit marital status discrimination in housing).
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; general national real estate licensing curriculum.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A property manager refuses to rent a two-bedroom apartment to a couple because they have a five-year-old child. This refusal is discrimination based on which protected class?
choice_a: Familial status
choice_b: National origin
choice_c: Disability
choice_d: Sex
explanation: Familial status protects households with one or more children under 18 living with a parent or legal guardian, as well as pregnant women and people in the process of securing legal custody of a minor.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3602(k); DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, which of the following is included within the definition of "familial status"?
choice_a: A pregnant woman who has not yet given birth
choice_b: Any household without children
choice_c: A married couple over age 62 with no dependents
choice_d: A single adult living alone
explanation: Familial status protection extends to households with children under 18, pregnant women, and anyone in the process of securing legal custody of a minor child, in addition to parents/guardians already living with minor children.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A leasing agent tells a prospective tenant born in Vietnam that no units are currently available, but tells a U.S.-born applicant the same day that a unit just opened up. If motivated by the applicant's birthplace, this is discrimination based on:
choice_a: National origin
choice_b: Religion
choice_c: Race
choice_d: Familial status
explanation: Discrimination based on a person's country of birth, ancestry, or culture is discrimination based on national origin, a protected class under the Fair Housing Act.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: An apartment community consistently declines to rent to applicants who wear religious head coverings. This practice violates the protected class of:
choice_a: Religion
choice_b: National origin
choice_c: Familial status
choice_d: Disability
explanation: Refusing housing based on an applicant's religious practices or observable religious dress is discrimination based on religion, one of the classes protected under the Fair Housing Act.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A mortgage lender denies a loan application specifically because the applicant is a woman, despite her qualifying income and credit. This is a violation of the protected class of:
choice_a: Sex
choice_b: Familial status
choice_c: National origin
choice_d: Disability
explanation: The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in housing and housing-related lending on the basis of sex; this includes disparate treatment of applicants because of gender as well as sexual harassment in housing.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604, 3605; DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, a "disability" (handicap) is generally defined as:
choice_a: A physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities
choice_b: Any medical diagnosis documented by a physician within the last year
choice_c: A condition that entitles the person to Social Security disability payments
choice_d: Any temporary illness lasting more than 30 days
explanation: The Act defines disability as a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, having a record of such impairment, or being regarded as having such impairment.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3602(h); HUD Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, which individual is specifically EXCLUDED from disability protections?
choice_a: A current user of illegal controlled substances
choice_b: A person recovering from past drug addiction
choice_c: A person with a hearing impairment
choice_d: A person with a mobility impairment who uses a wheelchair
explanation: Current, illegal use of a controlled substance is expressly excluded from the definition of disability under the Fair Housing Act, along with certain sex offenders. Recovering addicts and individuals with physical or sensory impairments remain protected.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3602(h); DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which of the following describes the "Mrs. Murphy" exemption to the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: An owner-occupied building with no more than four units, where the owner lives in one of the units
choice_b: Any single-family home sold without a broker
choice_c: Housing operated exclusively for persons 62 and older
choice_d: A private club that only rents to its own members
explanation: The Mrs. Murphy exemption applies to owner-occupied dwellings containing living quarters for no more than four families, where the owner actually occupies one of the units.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(2); Wikipedia, Civil Rights Act of 1968 (Title VIII) summary of exemptions.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Even where the Mrs. Murphy owner-occupied exemption applies, which practice remains prohibited?
choice_a: Publishing a discriminatory advertisement stating a preference based on a protected class
choice_b: Charging any amount of rent the owner chooses
choice_c: Requiring a security deposit
choice_d: Requiring proof of income
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's ban on discriminatory advertising applies even to otherwise exempt transactions, such as the Mrs. Murphy owner-occupied exemption and the private-owner single-family home exemption.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b), 3604(c); DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A private individual owner wants to sell a single-family home without triggering full Fair Housing Act coverage. Which condition is required for the private-owner exemption to apply?
choice_a: The owner does not use a real estate broker and does not publish any discriminatory advertisement
choice_b: The buyer must be a family member
choice_c: The home must be sold for cash only
choice_d: The home must be vacant at the time of sale
explanation: The private single-family-home exemption applies only when the owner does not own more than a limited number of such homes at one time, does not use a real estate licensee's services, and does not use discriminatory advertising.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(1); DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A religious organization owns and operates non-commercial housing. Under the Fair Housing Act, this organization may generally:
choice_a: Give preference to members of its own religion, as long as membership itself is not restricted based on race, color, or national origin
choice_b: Refuse housing to anyone of a different race regardless of religious affiliation
choice_c: Charge higher rent to non-members without limitation
choice_d: Refuse housing to families with children without any age-restriction requirements
explanation: The religious organization exemption allows preference for its own members in non-commercial housing it owns or operates, provided the organization's membership is not itself restricted based on race, color, or national origin.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(a); DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act's private club exemption, a bona fide private club may:
choice_a: Limit occupancy of lodgings it owns or operates for other than a commercial purpose to its own members
choice_b: Discriminate in any commercial rental it operates, even if open to the general public
choice_c: Refuse membership based on race and still limit lodging to members
choice_d: Charge non-members more than members for identical commercial apartments
explanation: The private club exemption is narrow: it applies only to non-commercial lodgings owned or operated by a bona fide private club for the benefit of its own members, not to commercial housing open to the public.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(a); DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A housing community wants to qualify as "housing for older persons" under the 55-and-older exemption from familial status discrimination. Which requirement must it meet?
choice_a: At least 80 percent of occupied units must have at least one occupant age 55 or older, and the community must publish and adhere to policies demonstrating that intent
choice_b: Every unit must be occupied solely by persons 55 or older
choice_c: The community must exclude all persons under age 40 regardless of household composition
choice_d: The community need only advertise itself as a retirement community
explanation: The Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA) 55-and-older exemption requires at least 80% of occupied units to have at least one resident 55 or older, along with published policies and procedures and compliance with HUD's age-verification requirements.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b); Wikipedia, Housing for Older Persons Act.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: How does the "62-and-older" housing exemption under HOPA differ from the "55-and-older" exemption?
choice_a: The 62-and-older exemption requires that the housing be intended for, and solely occupied by, persons 62 or older, with no 80% threshold
choice_b: The 62-and-older exemption has no age verification requirement at all
choice_c: The 62-and-older exemption allows families with children if a grandparent lives there
choice_d: There is no meaningful difference between the two exemptions
explanation: Unlike the 55-and-older exemption (80% occupancy threshold plus published policies), the 62-and-older exemption is stricter, requiring the housing to be intended for and solely occupied by persons 62 years of age or older.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b); Wikipedia, Housing for Older Persons Act.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which of the following exemptions from the Fair Housing Act protects ONLY against familial status claims, and not against claims based on race, sex, religion, or the other protected classes?
choice_a: The housing for older persons (HOPA) exemption
choice_b: The Mrs. Murphy owner-occupied exemption
choice_c: The religious organization exemption
choice_d: The private club exemption
explanation: The HOPA exemption removes only familial status protections for qualifying senior housing; such communities remain fully subject to the Act's protections against race, color, religion, sex, national origin, and disability discrimination.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b); HUD guidance on housing for older persons.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: "Blockbusting" is best described as:
choice_a: Inducing owners to sell or rent by suggesting that persons of a particular protected class are moving into the neighborhood, in order to profit from the resulting panic selling
choice_b: Refusing to make loans on properties located in a particular neighborhood
choice_c: Steering buyers away from certain neighborhoods based on race
choice_d: Requiring a large down payment on properties in a declining market
explanation: Blockbusting is the practice of inducing panic selling by suggesting that the entry of persons of a particular race or other protected class into a neighborhood will lower property values, so the blockbuster can buy low and resell at a profit. It is expressly prohibited by the Fair Housing Act.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(e); Wikipedia, Blockbusting.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A licensee cold-calls homeowners in a racially changing neighborhood, warning that property values will soon fall and urging them to list their homes quickly at a discount. This conduct is an example of:
choice_a: Blockbusting
choice_b: Redlining
choice_c: Steering
choice_d: A legitimate market analysis
explanation: Soliciting panic sales by implying that the racial composition of a neighborhood is changing and will hurt values is a textbook example of blockbusting, prohibited under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(e).
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(e); Wikipedia, Blockbusting.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: "Steering" refers to the practice of:
choice_a: Directing prospective buyers or renters toward or away from particular neighborhoods based on a protected class
choice_b: Refusing to lend money in a specific geographic area
choice_c: Charging different commission rates to different sellers
choice_d: Advising a buyer to consider a wider range of neighborhoods regardless of price
explanation: Steering occurs when an agent influences a buyer's or renter's housing choices by limiting or directing the options shown based on race or another protected class, effectively perpetuating segregation.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A buyer's agent, without being asked, only shows a Latino family listings in neighborhoods that are predominantly Latino, while showing comparable White families listings across many different neighborhoods. This is an example of:
choice_a: Steering
choice_b: Redlining
choice_c: A permissible marketing strategy
choice_d: Blockbusting
explanation: Limiting the neighborhoods shown to a buyer based on their race or national origin, rather than their stated preferences and budget, is steering, a violation of the Fair Housing Act.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; DOJ Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: "Redlining" traditionally refers to which discriminatory practice?
choice_a: Lenders or insurers denying or limiting services, such as mortgages or homeowners insurance, in specific neighborhoods based on the racial or ethnic composition of residents
choice_b: An agent showing a buyer only listings in one part of town
choice_c: A seller refusing to negotiate price with a particular buyer
choice_d: An appraiser overvaluing a property to secure a larger loan
explanation: Redlining is the practice, historically by lenders and insurers, of drawing a figurative red line around certain neighborhoods (often based on racial composition) and denying or limiting credit, insurance, or other services there.
source_note: Wikipedia, Redlining; 42 U.S.C. § 3605 (real estate-related transactions).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Although redlining is most closely associated with lenders and insurers, a real estate licensee could still face fair housing liability for redlining-type conduct if the licensee:
choice_a: Consistently refers minority clients only to lenders known for less favorable terms based on the client's race
choice_b: Recommends the same lender to every client regardless of race
choice_c: Discloses all available financing options to every client equally
choice_d: Declines to recommend any specific lender to any client
explanation: Real estate-related transactions, including referrals for financing, are covered by the Fair Housing Act; steering clients toward inferior lenders or terms based on a protected class can expose a licensee to liability even though redlining is traditionally a lending-industry practice.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3605; HUD Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, discriminatory advertising is prohibited when an advertisement:
choice_a: Indicates a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class
choice_b: Uses more than two adjectives to describe the property
choice_c: Fails to list the exact square footage
choice_d: Includes a photograph of the property's exterior
explanation: The Act makes it unlawful to publish any advertisement for the sale or rental of a dwelling that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class, regardless of the advertiser's actual intent.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); HUD Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which of the following advertising phrases would most likely violate the Fair Housing Act's advertising provisions?
choice_a: "Perfect for a mature working couple, no kids"
choice_b: "Spacious two-bedroom with updated kitchen"
choice_c: "Walking distance to public transit"
choice_d: "Freshly painted, move-in ready"
explanation: "No kids" expresses a preference against familial status, and "mature" can imply an age preference; such language signals a discriminatory preference and violates the FHA's advertising provisions, unlike neutral descriptions of the property itself.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); HUD Fair Housing Advertising guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Real estate advertisements commonly display the Equal Housing Opportunity logo or slogan primarily in order to:
choice_a: Communicate the advertiser's commitment to comply with fair housing laws and not discriminate
choice_b: Satisfy state licensing continuing education requirements
choice_c: Qualify the property for a lower property tax assessment
choice_d: Meet MLS data entry field requirements only
explanation: Displaying the Equal Housing Opportunity logo, slogan, or statement signals that housing is offered without regard to protected class, consistent with HUD's fair housing advertising and marketing guidance.
source_note: HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines; 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Do the Fair Housing Act's advertising prohibitions apply to listings posted on internet platforms and social media, not just print or MLS listings?
choice_a: Yes, the prohibition on discriminatory advertising applies regardless of the medium used
choice_b: No, only printed newspaper advertisements are covered
choice_c: No, social media posts are considered personal speech and exempt
choice_d: Only paid advertisements are covered, not organic posts
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's ban on discriminatory statements or preferences in housing advertisements applies across all media, including online listing platforms and social media, not just traditional print ads.
source_note: HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines; HUD enforcement actions against online ad-targeting practices.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: What is a "reasonable accommodation" for a person with a disability under the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: A change in rules, policies, practices, or services to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling
choice_b: A structural modification to the interior of a unit made at the tenant's own expense
choice_c: A reduction in rent for tenants with disabilities
choice_d: A requirement that all units be built with wider doorways
explanation: A reasonable accommodation is a change in rules, policies, practices, or services (for example, waiving a no-pets policy to allow an assistance animal) so a person with a disability has equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B); HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: What is a "reasonable modification" for a person with a disability under the Fair Housing Act, as distinguished from a reasonable accommodation?
choice_a: A structural or physical change to a dwelling or common area, such as a wheelchair ramp, which the tenant may be required to pay for in private housing
choice_b: A change to the landlord's pet policy
choice_c: A change to the rent due date
choice_d: A change to a lease's occupancy limit
explanation: A reasonable modification is a physical or structural change to the premises (like a ramp or grab bars). Unlike a reasonable accommodation (a policy change), the landlord in privately owned, non-federally-assisted housing may require the tenant to pay for the modification.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A); HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Modifications.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A tenant with a mobility impairment asks to install grab bars in the bathroom at her own expense. The landlord must:
choice_a: Permit the reasonable modification, since refusing would violate the Fair Housing Act
choice_b: Deny the request because it would alter the unit
choice_c: Require the tenant to move to a different unit instead
choice_d: Charge the tenant an additional non-refundable disability fee
explanation: Landlords must permit reasonable, tenant-requested structural modifications necessary for a person with a disability to fully use the dwelling; in private housing, the landlord may require the tenant to bear the reasonable cost.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A); HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Modifications.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: What does the acronym "ADA" stand for, and what is its general purpose?
choice_a: The Americans with Disabilities Act, a federal civil rights law prohibiting discrimination against people with disabilities
choice_b: The Advertising Disclosure Act, governing real estate marketing
choice_c: The Agency Disclosure Act, governing broker representation
choice_d: The Appraisal Development Act, governing appraiser licensing
explanation: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq., is a federal civil rights law prohibiting discrimination against individuals with disabilities in employment, government services, and public accommodations.
source_note: ADA.gov, Introduction to the ADA; 42 U.S.C. § 12101.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which title of the ADA requires employers with 15 or more employees to provide equal employment opportunity to qualified individuals with disabilities?
choice_a: Title I
choice_b: Title II
choice_c: Title III
choice_d: Title IV
explanation: ADA Title I covers employment and applies to employers with 15 or more employees, requiring reasonable accommodations for qualified employees and applicants with disabilities, such as within a real estate brokerage's own office.
source_note: ADA.gov, Introduction to the ADA; 42 U.S.C. § 12111 et seq.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which title of the ADA covers programs and services provided by state and local governments, such as a public housing authority?
choice_a: Title II
choice_b: Title I
choice_c: Title III
choice_d: Title VIII
explanation: ADA Title II covers state and local government entities and their programs and services, including public housing authorities and government-operated facilities.
source_note: ADA.gov, Introduction to the ADA.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A real estate brokerage's public office and a builder's model home open to prospective buyers are generally covered under which title of the ADA?
choice_a: Title III, covering public accommodations and commercial facilities
choice_b: Title I, covering employment only
choice_c: Title II, covering government entities only
choice_d: The ADA does not apply to real estate offices or model homes
explanation: ADA Title III requires businesses that serve the public, including real estate offices and model homes open to prospective customers, to provide people with disabilities equal opportunity to access their goods and services.
source_note: ADA.gov, Introduction to the ADA (Title III public accommodations).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: For an EXISTING place of public accommodation (as opposed to new construction), the ADA generally requires the removal of physical barriers to access when doing so is:
choice_a: "Readily achievable," meaning easily accomplishable without much difficulty or expense
choice_b: Required regardless of cost or feasibility
choice_c: Optional at the business owner's sole discretion
choice_d: Only required if a lawsuit has already been filed
explanation: Under ADA Title III, existing facilities must remove architectural barriers when it is "readily achievable" to do so; new construction and alterations, by contrast, must meet the ADA Standards for Accessible Design.
source_note: ADA.gov, Introduction to the ADA; ADA Title III Primer.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the ADA, a covered business may generally ask about a service animal only two questions: whether the animal is required because of a disability, and:
choice_a: What work or task the animal has been trained to perform
choice_b: What breed the animal is
choice_c: For medical documentation proving the disability
choice_d: For proof the animal has completed a certification program
explanation: Under the ADA, staff may ask only (1) whether the animal is required because of a disability and (2) what work or task it has been trained to perform. Businesses may not require documentation, certification, or proof of training.
source_note: ADA.gov Service Animal guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the ADA, a "service animal" is generally limited to:
choice_a: A dog (and in some cases a miniature horse) individually trained to perform tasks for a person with a disability
choice_b: Any animal that provides comfort to its owner
choice_c: Any animal listed on a doctor's note
choice_d: Cats and dogs equally, with no training requirement
explanation: The ADA defines a service animal narrowly as a dog (with miniature horses accommodated in some circumstances) individually trained to perform specific tasks for a person with a disability, which is narrower than the broader "assistance animal" concept used under the Fair Housing Act.
source_note: ADA.gov Service Animal guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: How does the Fair Housing Act's concept of an "assistance animal" compare to the ADA's definition of a "service animal"?
choice_a: The FHA's assistance animal concept is broader, and can include animals other than dogs and animals that provide emotional support rather than task-based work
choice_b: The two definitions are identical in every respect
choice_c: The FHA definition is narrower and excludes emotional support animals entirely
choice_d: The FHA does not recognize assistance animals at all
explanation: Under the Fair Housing Act, an "assistance animal" is broader than the ADA's "service animal" — it is not limited to dogs and can include animals that provide emotional support, so long as there is a disability-related need, even without specialized task training.
source_note: HUD Assistance Animal Notice (FHEO-2020-01); ADA.gov Service Animal guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A rental community has a strict "no pets" policy. A tenant with a documented disability-related need requests to keep an assistance animal. The property manager should:
choice_a: Grant the request as a reasonable accommodation and waive the no-pets policy and any pet fee for the assistance animal
choice_b: Deny the request because the policy applies to all tenants equally
choice_c: Charge a standard pet deposit for the assistance animal
choice_d: Require the tenant to move to a different property that allows pets
explanation: An assistance animal is not a "pet" for Fair Housing Act purposes; a housing provider generally must grant a reasonable accommodation waiving a no-pets policy and may not charge a pet fee or deposit for the assistance animal.
source_note: HUD Assistance Animal Notice (FHEO-2020-01); 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The Sherman Antitrust Act, which underlies real estate antitrust rules, is codified at:
choice_a: 15 U.S.C. § 1 et seq.
choice_b: 42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.
choice_c: 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.
explanation: The Sherman Antitrust Act is codified at 15 U.S.C. § 1 et seq. and prohibits contracts, combinations, and conspiracies that unreasonably restrain trade, including certain conduct among competing real estate brokerages.
source_note: Wikipedia, Sherman Antitrust Act; 15 U.S.C. § 1.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under antitrust law, a "per se" violation is one where:
choice_a: The conduct is presumed illegal without any need to prove actual harm to competition in the market
choice_b: The plaintiff must prove significant economic harm before any liability attaches
choice_c: Only criminal penalties, never civil liability, can result
choice_d: The conduct is legal as long as no consumer complains
explanation: Per se violations, such as horizontal price fixing, market allocation, and group boycotts among competitors, are considered so inherently harmful to competition that they are treated as automatically illegal, with no need to analyze actual market effects.
source_note: Wikipedia, Sherman Antitrust Act (per se violations).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Several competing brokers in the same market meet informally and agree they will all charge sellers the same 6% commission rate. This conduct is an example of:
choice_a: Price fixing, a per se violation of antitrust law
choice_b: A legitimate industry standard
choice_c: Market allocation
choice_d: A group boycott
explanation: An agreement among competing brokers to charge the same commission rate is horizontal price fixing, a per se violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act, regardless of whether the agreed-upon rate is otherwise reasonable.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1; Wikipedia, Sherman Antitrust Act; NAR antitrust compliance guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: May two independently owned real estate brokerages each set their own commission rates without violating antitrust law?
choice_a: Yes, each brokerage may independently determine its own commission rates; the antitrust violation arises only from an agreement between competitors
choice_b: No, all brokerages must charge an identical commission rate set by the local association
choice_c: No, brokers may never discuss commissions with clients
choice_d: Yes, but only if the local MLS approves the rate first
explanation: Commission rates are always negotiable, and each brokerage may independently decide its own rates. Antitrust liability arises when competitors agree with each other on rates, not from independently set pricing.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1; NAR antitrust compliance guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Two competing brokerages agree that one will only list and sell properties on the north side of town while the other confines its business to the south side, so neither competes in the other's area. This is an example of:
choice_a: Market allocation (division of markets), a per se antitrust violation
choice_b: Steering, a fair housing violation
choice_c: A legitimate franchise territory agreement
choice_d: Blockbusting
explanation: An agreement between competitors to divide up geographic territories or customer types so they do not compete with each other is market allocation, a per se violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1; Wikipedia, Sherman Antitrust Act.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A group of established brokers collectively agree to deny multiple listing service access to a new discount brokerage that charges lower commissions. This is an example of:
choice_a: A group boycott, a per se antitrust violation
choice_b: Redlining
choice_c: Legitimate MLS membership screening
choice_d: Blockbusting
explanation: A concerted, collective refusal by competitors to deal with or cooperate with another market participant (such as denying MLS access to a discount broker) is a group boycott, a per se violation of antitrust law.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1; Wikipedia, Sherman Antitrust Act; NAR antitrust compliance guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: What kinds of penalties can result from a real estate antitrust violation such as price fixing?
choice_a: Both criminal penalties (fines and imprisonment) and civil liability (including treble damages) can apply
choice_b: Only a written warning from the local Realtor association
choice_c: Only loss of MLS access, with no other consequence
choice_d: Antitrust violations carry no meaningful penalty in real estate
explanation: Sherman Act violations can result in criminal prosecution (fines and imprisonment for individuals and firms) as well as civil antitrust suits, in which successful private plaintiffs may recover treble (triple) damages.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. § 1-2; Wikipedia, Sherman Antitrust Act.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: To reduce antitrust risk, real estate licensees are generally advised to avoid which topic when speaking with agents from competing firms?
choice_a: Commission rates, fees, or terms that their respective firms charge
choice_b: General real estate market conditions
choice_c: Changes to state licensing law
choice_d: New construction trends in the area
explanation: Discussing commission rates, fees charged, or similar competitively sensitive terms with agents at competing firms creates significant antitrust risk, since such conversations can be used as evidence of an unlawful agreement.
source_note: NAR antitrust compliance guidance; 15 U.S.C. § 1.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Do fair housing protections apply equally to rental property management, not just to home sales?
choice_a: Yes, the Fair Housing Act applies to the rental, as well as the sale, of covered dwellings, including tenant screening and property management practices
choice_b: No, the Fair Housing Act applies only to home sales
choice_c: No, property managers are exempt from fair housing law
choice_d: Fair housing law applies only to single-family rentals, not apartment communities
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's prohibitions apply broadly to housing transactions, including rentals and day-to-day property management functions such as tenant screening, showing units, and setting lease terms.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604; HUD Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: To comply with fair housing law, a property manager screening rental applicants should:
choice_a: Apply the same written screening criteria (such as income, credit, and rental history standards) uniformly to every applicant
choice_b: Use different credit score minimums depending on the applicant's national origin
choice_c: Ask only applicants of certain races for additional references
choice_d: Waive screening criteria for applicants the manager personally prefers
explanation: Consistent, uniformly applied written screening criteria for all applicants helps ensure decisions are based on legitimate business criteria rather than a protected class, reducing fair housing risk.
source_note: HUD Fair Housing Act overview; general national property management practice.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: In a typical property management arrangement, the property manager acts as agent for:
choice_a: The property owner/landlord, under a written property management agreement
choice_b: The tenant exclusively
choice_c: Neither party, acting only as a neutral facilitator
choice_d: The local housing authority
explanation: A property manager is typically engaged under a management agreement to act as the agent of the property owner, owing the owner fiduciary duties while managing leasing, maintenance, and rent collection.
source_note: General national real estate licensing curriculum on property management agency.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: As agent for the property owner, a property manager generally owes the owner which set of fiduciary duties?
choice_a: Loyalty, obedience to lawful instructions, full disclosure, confidentiality, reasonable care and skill, and accounting for funds
choice_b: Duties owed only to the tenant, not the owner
choice_c: No fiduciary duties, since property management is a purely ministerial role
choice_d: A duty to maximize rent regardless of legal restrictions
explanation: As an agent, a property manager owes the owner-client the traditional fiduciary duties commonly summarized as loyalty, obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, reasonable care/skill, and accounting.
source_note: General national real estate licensing curriculum on agency/fiduciary duties.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Rent and security deposit funds collected by a property manager on behalf of an owner should generally be:
choice_a: Kept in a separate trust or client-funds account, not commingled with the manager's own operating funds
choice_b: Deposited directly into the property manager's personal checking account
choice_c: Held in cash on the property manager's premises
choice_d: Immediately paid out to the manager as a fee before any owner disbursement
explanation: As a matter of fiduciary duty and standard trust-accounting practice, client funds such as collected rents and security deposits must be held in a separate trust/client account rather than commingled with the manager's own funds.
source_note: General national real estate licensing curriculum on trust accounting/commingling.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A property management company manages several apartment communities. Under the ADA, common areas of these properties open to the public, such as a leasing office, should generally:
choice_a: Provide accessible routes and features consistent with Title III's public accommodation requirements
choice_b: Be exempt from ADA requirements because they are residential in nature
choice_c: Only need to comply if a tenant specifically requests it
choice_d: Be governed exclusively by the Fair Housing Act, with no ADA application at all
explanation: Public-facing common areas such as leasing offices are commercial facilities/public accommodations under ADA Title III, while the dwelling units themselves are primarily governed by the Fair Housing Act's design and construction requirements.
source_note: ADA.gov, Introduction to the ADA (Title III); 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C) design/construction requirements.
